In [[mathematics]], a '''bundle map''' (or '''bundle [[morphism]]''') is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] that relates two [[fiber bundles]] in a way that respects their internal structure. Fiber bundles are mathematical objects that locally look like a [[cartesian product]] of a base space and another space, the typical "fiber", but may have more complex global structure.

A bundle map typically consists of two functions: one between the [[total space]]s of the bundles, and one between their base spaces, such that the [[commutative diagram|diagram]] formed by the projections commutes. In some cases, both bundles share the same base space, and in others, the map includes a separate function between different base spaces.

There are several versions of bundle maps depending on the specific types of fiber bundles involved—for example, smooth bundles, [[vector bundle]]s, or [[principal bundle]]s—and on the category in which they are defined (e.g., [[topological space]]s or [[smooth manifold]]s).

The first three sections of this article discusses general fiber bundles in the [[category of topological spaces]], while the fourth section provides other examples.

==Bundle maps over a common base==
Let <math>\pi_E\colon E \to M</math> and <math>\pi_F\colon F \to M</math> be fiber bundles over a space ''M''. Then a '''bundle map from ''E'' to ''F'' over ''M''''' is a continuous map <math>\varphi\colon E \to F</math> such that <math> \pi_F\circ\varphi = \pi_E </math>. That is, the diagram
{{Dark mode invert|[[Image:BundleMorphism-03.svg|120px|center]]}}

should [[commutative diagram|commute]]. Equivalently, for any point ''x'' in ''M'', <math>\varphi</math> maps the fiber <math>E_x= \pi_E^{-1}(\{x\})</math> of ''E'' over ''x'' to the fiber <math>F_x= \pi_F^{-1}(\{x\})</math> of ''F'' over ''x''.<ref>[[#refHusemoller1994|Husemoller, ''Fibre bundles'']], Definition 3.2</ref>

==General morphisms of fiber bundles==
Let π<sub>''E''</sub>:''E''→ ''M'' and π<sub>''F''</sub>:''F''→ ''N'' be fiber bundles over spaces ''M'' and ''N'' respectively. Then a continuous map <math>\varphi : E \to F</math> is called a '''bundle map''' from ''E'' to ''F'' if there is a continuous map ''f'':''M''→ ''N'' such that the diagram
{{Dark mode invert|[[Image:BundleMorphism-04.svg|150px|center]]}}

commutes, that is, <math> \pi_F\circ\varphi = f\circ\pi_E </math>. In other words, <math>\varphi</math> is '''fiber-preserving''', and ''f'' is the induced map on the space of fibers of ''E'': since π<sub>''E''</sub> is surjective, ''f'' is uniquely determined by <math>\varphi</math>. For a given ''f'', such a bundle map <math>\varphi</math> is  said to be a '''bundle map ''covering f'''''.<ref>[[#refHusemoller1994|Husemoller, ''Fibre bundles'']], Definition 3.2</ref>

==Relation between the two notions==
It follows immediately from the definitions that a bundle map over ''M'' (in the first sense) is the same thing as a bundle map covering the identity map of ''M''.

Conversely, general bundle maps can be reduced to bundle maps over a fixed base space using the notion of a [[pullback bundle]]. If π<sub>''F''</sub>:''F''→ ''N'' is a fiber bundle over ''N'' and ''f'':''M''→ ''N'' is a continuous map, then the '''pullback''' of ''F'' by ''f'' is a fiber bundle ''f''<sup>*</sup>''F'' over ''M'' whose fiber over ''x'' is given by (''f''<sup>*</sup>''F'')<sub>''x''</sub> = ''F''<sub>''f''(''x'')</sub>. It then follows that a bundle map from ''E'' to ''F'' covering ''f'' is the same thing as a bundle map from ''E'' to ''f''<sup>*</sup>''F'' over ''M''.

==Variants and generalizations==
There are two kinds of variation of the general notion of a bundle map.

First, one can consider fiber bundles in a different category of spaces. This leads, for example, to the notion of a '''smooth bundle map''' between smooth fiber bundles over a [[smooth manifold]].

Second, one can consider fiber bundles with extra structure in their fibers, and restrict attention to bundle maps which preserve this structure. This leads, for example, to the notion of a '''(vector) bundle homomorphism''' between [[vector bundle]]s, in which the fibers are vector spaces, and a bundle map ''φ'' is required to be a linear map on each fiber.<ref>[[#refLee2013|Lee, ''Introduction to smooth manifolds'']], Page 261</ref> In this case, such a bundle map ''φ'' (covering ''f'') may also be viewed as a [[section (fiber bundle)|section]] of the vector bundle Hom(''E'',''f<sup>*</sup>F'') over ''M'', whose fiber over ''x'' is the [[vector space]] Hom(''E<sub>x</sub>'',''F''<sub>''f''(''x'')</sub>) (also denoted ''L''(''E<sub>x</sub>'',''F''<sub>''f''(''x'')</sub>)) of [[linear map]]s from 
''E<sub>x</sub>'' to ''F''<sub>''f''(''x'')</sub>.
